questions.q: Why is MlpPolicy an appropriate choice for this environment rather than a convolutional or sequence-based policy?
options: Because stable-baselines3 only offers MlpPolicy
Because the observation is just two features and the action space is Discrete(5) — no image or sequence to process
Because MlpPolicy is required for any environment using pyodbc
Because convolutional policies cannot output discrete actions
questions.explain: A small fully-connected network has more than enough capacity for a 2-feature observation and 5 discrete actions, with no spatial or sequential structure to exploit.

questions.q: Why does training use n_envs=4 to run multiple environment copies in parallel?
options: Because PPO requires at least four environments to function at all
Because every single step involves a real round-trip to SQL Server, unlike a cheap simulator step
Because the action space has four actions besides the no-hint action
Because stable-baselines3 cannot run with a single environment
questions.explain: Since each environment step executes real SQL against the sandbox, parallelizing across multiple environment copies matters more here than in environments with cheap simulated steps.

questions.q: What is the key similarity and the key difference between this project's PPO and Project 3's PPO?
options: They are different algorithms entirely, sharing only the name
Same algorithm family (PPO), but applied via a completely different library and modality — a small MLP over a feature vector here vs. a language model's token policy in Project 3
They are identical in every respect, including the policy architecture
Project 3 does not actually use PPO
questions.explain: Both use PPO as the underlying policy-gradient algorithm, but Project 1 uses stable-baselines3's MlpPolicy over a tabular observation, while Project 3 uses TRL's PPOTrainer over a language model's generation policy.

questions.q: How does the trained policy resolve the Lesson 1 notebook entry about FORCE ORDER?
options: It avoids FORCE ORDER entirely in every episode
It learns to pick FORCE ORDER selectively on wide date ranges, and a different hint on narrow ranges, instead of applying one hint everywhere
It always picks FORCE ORDER regardless of date range, just as attempt 2 did
It removes FORCE ORDER from the action space after training
questions.explain: The notebook's attempt 2 mistake was applying FORCE ORDER uniformly; the trained policy fixes this by conditioning its hint choice on date_range_days, matching the notebook's planned next step.

questions.q: What does it mean that 'PPO doesn't care whether the policy is a two-layer MLP or a multi-billion-parameter transformer'?
options: PPO can only be used with transformer architectures
PPO is a general policy-gradient method whose core update rule applies regardless of the policy network's architecture or scale
PPO automatically converts MLPs into transformers during training
PPO requires rewriting its algorithm for each new policy architecture
questions.explain: The lesson frames this as a deliberate compare/contrast: the same PPO algorithm underlies both a small tabular policy here and a full language-model policy in Project 3.
